title: Swedish breeding-bird communities followed 24-47% of their spatial temperature gradient in 1996-2025; species range edges moved about 35% in the steep-gradient north and not in the flat south
abstract: Question: which part of the spatial temperature gradient do Swedish breeding-bird communities follow in time, and where along the gradient does the gap arise? Data: Swedish Bird Survey fixed routes on a systematic 25-km grid (677 routes, 1996-2025, CC0), summer point-count routes (1975-2024), E-OBS April-June temperature, ESA WorldCover land cover, and European species temperature indices (STI) from GBIF June records. Methods: community temperature index (CTI) trend, window and year-to-year ratios to the spatial CTI slope with Sweden-internal and European STIs; two-edge occupancy models for 170 species, with edge shifts calibrated by simulation; route-cluster bootstrap. Results: CTI followed 26% (95% CI 21-32%) of the spatial slope with internal STIs and 39% (32-47%) with European STIs over the 30-year trend; window estimates were 27-47%. Year-to-year transfer was near zero (-0.4% and 1.0%). Internal STIs saturate at the warm end of the network and made a false north-south contrast (difference 0.36 versus 0.11 with European STIs). Land-cover adjustment reduced the spatial slope by only 12-19%, and southern farmland routes did not lag forest routes. Species range edges moved 15% (7-27%) of the shift that full tracking needs; edges below 8 C moved 35% (24-48%) and edges at 8 C or more did not move (-9%, -20 to 3%). Full tracking needed a median shift of 42 km in the north and 107 km in the flat south; realised shifts were 11 km and -15 km. After calibration, leading and trailing edges did not differ clearly. Southern community change came mostly from redwing and fieldfare declines. Limitations: one country and taxon; 25-km square coordinates; coarse GBIF-based STIs; the cause of the north-south edge contrast (distance, topography, community type) is not identified; attribution rests on regional trends, not local covariation.
